prompt.context: Our client, Tarrant Fixtures, is a low-intensity manufacturing company that produces display fixtures for retail clients. The company's financial performance has deteriorated in each of the last three years. Specifically, they are concerned with the company's falling Return on Investment (ROI). The CEO has asked us to look into this problem.
prompt.question: How can Tarrant Fixtures get back on track?

clarifying_info.q: What types of products does Tarrant make?
clarifying_info.a: Two types: Custom displays (50% of sales) — produced only when an order is placed and payment is received. Standard displays (50% of sales) — manufactured to open standards and stored in inventory (built-to-stock).

clarifying_info.q: How many standardized products are there?
clarifying_info.a: 5 standardized products account for 80% of standardized-product sales. The total number of standardized products increased from 5 to 12 over the last three years.

clarifying_info.q: How have revenues changed over the past three years?
clarifying_info.a: Total revenues grew 25%, from $100M to $125M, equally across both product types.
Costs of production (COGS, labor, SG&A, etc.) remained stable as a percentage of revenue at 80%.

clarifying_info.q: Has the company made any new capital investments?
clarifying_info.a: No. There has been no new investment in Property, Plant & Equipment (CAPEX = 0).

clarifying_info.q: What has happened to working capital?
clarifying_info.a: Total working capital employed was $80M three years ago and is $130M today — an increase of $50M. Inventory levels have increased by 300%, from $25M to $75M, primarily in finished goods.

clarifying_info.q: How has the market been growing?
clarifying_info.a: The market has grown 25% over the past three years.

clarifying_info.q: What is the client's market position?
clarifying_info.a: The client has remained the industry market share leader in displays, maintaining 25% market share over the past three years.

clarifying_info.q: What is the competitive environment like?
clarifying_info.a: There are several players in the market, but everything has remained stable from a competitive standpoint.

exhibits.title: Working Capital Statement
exhibits.shows: A line-by-line working capital statement listing the relevant categories of capital (e.g., inventory, accounts receivable, accounts payable, cash, PP&E) used to calculate capital employed for ROI purposes.
exhibits.data: Categories of working capital components; total working capital employed three years ago = $80M, today = $130M; inventory increased from $25M to $75M

framework: Define ROI and decompose into its two components: Net Profit (numerator) and Capital Employed (denominator)
Analyze Net Profit: examine revenue trends and cost structure to determine whether profit decline is driving the ROI drop
Analyze Capital Employed: break down working capital line by line (PP&E, inventory, AR, AP, cash) to identify what has grown
Deep-dive inventory: identify root causes of the $50M inventory build-up
Generate recommendations to reduce inventory and restore ROI

questions.prompt: What is the formula for ROI, and what does it tell us about where to look?
questions.guidance: ROI = Net Profit / Capital Employed. A falling ROI means either net profit fell, capital employed rose, or both. The candidate should propose examining both the numerator (profitability) and denominator (capital base) before diving in.

questions.prompt: Has net profit been declining? Calculate net profit for Year 1 and Year 3.
questions.guidance: Net profit has NOT declined in absolute or percentage terms — it has grown in line with revenue. This eliminates the numerator as the cause of the ROI issue and directs attention to the denominator.

math.setup: Net Profit = Revenue × (1 - Cost % of Revenue). Cost % = 80% in both years.
steps: Net profit grew 25%, in line with revenue — not the problem
math.answer: Net profit grew from $20M to $25M (+25%). Profit is not the cause of the falling ROI.

questions.prompt: What has happened to capital employed? Use the working capital exhibit to identify the culprit.
questions.guidance: PP&E is constant (no CAPEX). All other working capital items (AR, AP, cash) are stable. Inventory is the only line that changed materially — it increased $50M, which fully explains the $50M increase in total working capital. The candidate should pinpoint inventory as the root cause.

math.setup: Total Working Capital change = Today ($130M) - Three years ago ($80M) = +$50M. Inventory change = $75M - $25M = +$50M (300% increase).
steps: PP&E, AR, AP, and cash are all stable
Therefore inventory accounts for 100% of the capital employed increase
math.answer: The entire $50M increase in capital employed is due to inventory build-up, entirely in finished goods (standard displays).

questions.prompt: What are the likely root causes of the inventory increase?
questions.guidance: Strong answers identify: (1) SKU proliferation — standard product lines grew from 5 to 12 SKUs over three years, increasing the total stock that must be held; (2) inaccurate demand forecasts leading to excess safety stock; (3) obsolete inventories from discontinued or slow-moving product lines.

brainstorming.prompt: What can management do to reduce inventory and prevent future build-up?

categories.name: Rationalize product lines
ideas: Reduce standard product SKUs back to the top 5 products (which account for 80% of standardized-product sales)
Institute a formal SKU governance process to evaluate new product additions against inventory cost implications

categories.name: Improve demand forecasting
ideas: Implement statistical forecasting tools to set more accurate safety stock levels
Use point-of-sale data from retail clients to enable pull-based replenishment
Establish regular forecast review cycles with sales and operations planning (S&OP)

categories.name: Manage obsolete inventory
ideas: Write off or mark down obsolete finished goods (note: this will cause an immediate profit hit, so management may be reluctant)
Run promotions or offer discounts to work down excess stock
Set a formal inventory aging policy with automatic markdown triggers

categories.name: Structural / process changes
ideas: Shift more standard-display demand to a make-to-order or postponement model to reduce finished goods risk
Improve production flexibility to respond faster to demand signals with smaller batch sizes
Align incentives — ensure sales and operations teams are not rewarded in ways that encourage inventory build-up

recommendation: The client's ROI has fallen because a $50M increase in working capital (driven entirely by a 300% inventory increase) expanded the capital employed denominator while net profit grew only modestly. To restore ROI, Tarrant must reduce finished-goods inventory by rationalizing its standard-product line back to the top 5 SKUs, improving demand forecasting accuracy, and writing off or working down obsolete inventory.
risks: Writing off obsolete inventory will cause an immediate negative impact on reported profits, which management may resist
Cutting SKUs from 12 back to 5 could affect customer relationships if some clients depend on the discontinued products
Improving forecast accuracy requires investment in systems and process change that takes time to deliver results
next_steps: Conduct a detailed SKU-level profitability analysis to confirm which 7 standard products to discontinue
Build a demand-forecasting improvement roadmap with a target safety-stock reduction
Quantify the write-off impact of obsolete inventory and develop a board communication plan
Set a target ROI and track progress quarterly against a working-capital reduction milestones
